orient: Jewel, the brother Darl just described at the barn. Instead of a scene, this section is one furious rush of thought in run-on sentences: anger at Cash for building the coffin under their mother's window, and at the neighbours watching her die.

notes.n: Like Darl, Jewel won't say the word 'coffin'.

notes.t: saying See. See what a good one I am making for you.
notes.g: Jewel imagines what Cash is 'saying' with every stroke.
notes.n: Faulkner prints spoken or imagined words without quotation marks. A capital letter mid-sentence (See, Good God) shows where the words begin.

notes.t: I said Good God do you want to see her in it.
notes.g: What Jewel told Cash: 'Good God, do you want to see her in it?'
notes.n: Again the speech is run straight into the sentence, with no quotation marks or question mark.
'Taken' for 'took' is common in rural Southern speech.
Jewel sneers at Cash's eagerness to please their mother, even as a boy.

notes.g: Like vultures waiting for something to die.
notes.n: Turkey buzzards are a common sight in the rural South. Jewel sees the visitors as birds waiting for a death.
Her hands are so thin and knotted they look like roots dug out of the ground.

notes.g: Dewey Dell is the Bundren daughter: the 'tom-boy girl' fanning her mother in Section 2.

notes.n: A 'lick' is a blow or stroke. Each stroke of the adze brings the coffin, and in Jewel's mind his mother's death, one step closer.

notes.s: If it had just been me when Cash fell off of that church
notes.e: One lick less and we could be quiet.
notes.tr: If it had only been me with her, back when Cash fell off that church and when Pa lay sick after that load of wood fell on him, none of this would be happening, with every so-and-so in the county coming in to stare at her. Because if there is a God, what the hell is He for? It would be just me and her on a high hill, and me rolling rocks down the hill at their faces, picking them up and throwing them down, faces and teeth and all, by God, until she had peace. Instead of that damned adze going one stroke less, one stroke less, and then we could be quiet.
notes.n: 'If it had just been me' is ambiguous. One common reading: Jewel wishes it were only him and his mother, with nobody else around. The next sentence ('just me and her on a high hill') supports it.

notes.t: when Cash fell off of that church
notes.g: Cash once fell from the roof of a church he was working on.
notes.n: An accident from the family's past, mentioned in passing.

notes.t: pa laid sick with that load of wood fell on him
notes.g: Pa lay sick after a load of wood fell on him.
notes.n: Southern speech often drops 'that' or 'after' and joins the clauses directly.
